slide_title: Human Cardiovascular System: Blood Pressure & Flow
original_text: Human Cardiovascular System Blood Pressure Contraction of the heart supplies pressure that keeps blood moving in the arteries Systolic pressure results from blood forced into the arteries during ventricular systole Diastolic pressure is the pressure in the arteries during ventricular diastole Sphygmomanometer on brachial artery Systole/Diastole In arteries, the pressure of the blood forces it to move forward Blood pressure falls as blood flows from the aorta into arteries and arterioles Blood flow in the capillaries is slow Blood pressure in the veins is too low to move blood back to the heart Skeletal muscle contraction pushes blood in the veins toward the heart Veins have valves to prevent backward flow of blood A respiratory pump reduces pressure in the thoracic cavity to cause blood to move from the abdominal cavity into the thoracic cavity
explanation: Heart contraction provides the blood pressure that keeps blood moving. Blood pressure is measured on the brachial artery using a sphygmomanometer and is written as systolic pressure (during ventricular contraction) over diastolic pressure (during ventricular relaxation). Blood pressure falls continuously as blood flows from the aorta to the arteries and arterioles, and blood flow velocity is slowest in capillaries to allow material exchange. Because venous blood pressure is very low, three mechanisms assist in returning blood to the heart: 1) Skeletal muscle contractions that compress veins, 2) One-way venous valves that prevent backflow, and 3) A respiratory pump that decreases thoracic cavity pressure during inhalation to pull blood up from the abdomen.

questions.q: How is diastolic blood pressure defined?
opts: The blood pressure in arteries during ventricular contraction (systole)
The blood pressure in arteries during ventricular relaxation (diastole)
The pressure wave passing down the walls of veins
The pressure measured in the lymphatic vessels
questions.exp: Diastolic pressure is the baseline pressure in the arteries when the ventricles are relaxing (diastole).

questions.q: Why does blood flow slowly in the capillaries?
opts: To allow adequate time for the exchange of nutrients, gases, and wastes
Because capillaries are under the direct control of the SA node
Due to the presence of thick elastic walls and valves
questions.exp: The velocity of blood flow is slowest in capillaries to maximize the efficiency of material diffusion between blood and tissues.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a mechanism that assists in returning venous blood to the heart?
opts: High pressure generated by the right atrium
questions.exp: Venous blood is under very low pressure; it relies on skeletal muscle pumping, valves, and the respiratory pump, not right atrial pressure, to return to the heart.
